name: Palmitoyl tripeptide-5

lead: Palmitoyl tripeptide-5, sold as Syn-Coll, is a lab-made peptide attached to a fatty acid and added to anti-wrinkle and skin-firming creams, serums and microneedle patches. People use it for firmer, denser-looking skin and fewer wrinkles.

Suppliers describe it as a signal peptide that stimulates collagen synthesis through a TGF-beta-related pathway, with the fatty chain helping it cross the outer skin layer; this is mainly manufacturer description. Published studies have tested it in multi-ingredient products, such as hyaluronic acid microneedle patches loaded with several peptides, and no standalone placebo-controlled trial was found.

paras: It is used as a leave-on serum or cream, or in microneedle patches, often combined with other peptides and hydrating ingredients. Firmness and wrinkle changes are typically assessed over several weeks of daily use.
No specific safety problems are documented in the sources found. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug.

angle.text: Palmitoyl tripeptide-5 (Syn-Coll) is a collagen-signalling peptide used in creams, serums and microneedle patches for firmer skin and fewer wrinkles. It prompts skin cells to make collagen, which densifies the dermis. Published studies are small and use multi-ingredient products.

lead: Palmitoyl tripeptide-5, sold under the trade name Syn-Coll, is a synthetic lipopeptide used as an ingredient in anti-wrinkle and skin-firming cosmetics. It is marketed as a "signal peptide" intended to prompt skin cells to make more collagen, and it appears in creams, serums and microneedle patches.

Published material on the ingredient is mostly about multi-ingredient products. A 12-week clinical study tested hyaluronic acid microneedle patches loaded with several bioactives, including palmitoyl tripeptide-5, for tolerability and skin effects [1]. A 2025 laboratory and use study encapsulated it in collagen nanoparticles [2], and a 2021 review of cosmetics for sensitive skin found it among seven peptides in 88 products, noting that supporting data are mostly in patents and supplier brochures rather than placebo-controlled trials [3]. No published trial was found that isolates palmitoyl tripeptide-5 as a single active against placebo.

paras: The peptide is used in cosmetic products aimed at fine lines and loss of firmness. Manufacturers describe it as stimulating collagen production through a growth-factor-related signalling pathway (marketed as TGF-beta stimulation); these mechanism statements originate largely from supplier material rather than independent trials.

A 2021 review in Pharmaceuticals analysed the composition of 88 facial cosmetics for sensitive skin from multinational brands. Peptides were present in 17 percent of the products, and the seven identified were acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester, palmitoyl tripeptide-8, acetyl tetrapeptide-15, palmitoyl tripeptide-5, acetyl hexapeptide-49, palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 and palmitoyl oligopeptide. Three of the seven act by inhibiting neurotransmitters and three are signal peptides; only five had evidence for use in sensitive skin, with just one clinical study including volunteers with that condition, and the review noted that data are mostly in patents and supplier brochures [3].

The broader family of lipidated cosmetic peptides is illustrated by palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, sold as Matrixyl and launched in 2000 by the French manufacturer Sederma. Wikipedia describes that peptide as a matrikine, a messenger peptide with a 16-carbon fatty chain attached to help it penetrate skin lipids, and reports that the anti-wrinkle effect is claimed through boosting extracellular matrix synthesis [4]. Palmitoyl tripeptide-5 is marketed in the same signal-peptide tradition.

Suppliers describe the peptide as stimulating collagen through a growth-factor-related signal; a review of cosmetic peptides classes palmitoyl tripeptide-5 among the signal peptides rather than neurotransmitter inhibitors [3]. The palmitoyl group is a fatty acid attached to help peptides cross the skin's lipid barrier [4]. Whether peptides of this size reach the dermis is part of the research question: collagen-based products can have difficulty penetrating the dermis, which motivated nanoparticle work [2].

In a 2023 study of supramolecular hydrogels, two cosmetic peptides, trifluoroacetyl tripeptide-2 and palmitoyl tripeptide-5, were added to the gels and their transdermal permeation was analysed with Franz diffusion cells. Trifluoroacetyl tripeptide-2 permeated in a considerable amount, while almost no transdermal permeation of palmitoyl tripeptide-5 was observed in that system [5].

A monocentric 12-week clinical study examined hyaluronic acid microneedle patches loaded with arginine/lysine polypeptide, acetyl octapeptide-3, palmitoyl tripeptide-5, adenosine and seaweed extracts on healthy subjects with aged skin. Patches were applied at the outer corner of each eye and on a defined area of the forearm, with instrumental measures of hydration, wrinkle reduction, density and thickness. The product was tolerated excellently, with no primary or cumulative skin reactions reported [1]. Because the patch contained several actives and a microneedle delivery system, the results cannot be attributed to palmitoyl tripeptide-5 alone.

A 2025 study combined lactoferrin, recombinant human collagen and palmitoyl tripeptide-5 in supramolecular collagen nanoparticles, with an encapsulation rate of 94.18 percent. The authors reported improved transdermal efficiency (69.90 percent) and, over 28 days of use, increases in stratum corneum moisture (10.51 percent), facial elasticity (8.15 percent) and skin firmness (12.53 percent), with reductions in melanin index and, within 14 days, reductions in eye bag wrinkles (24.69 percent) and nasolabial wrinkles (37.61 percent) [2]. This is a multi-component formulation without a placebo-isolated peptide arm described in the abstract.

A registered trial of three Hydrafacial treatments assessed skin quality, hydration and barrier in 27 adults (NCT05932732) [6]; the registration does not by itself show a specific effect of this peptide. No published randomized trial isolates palmitoyl tripeptide-5 against placebo.

In the microneedle patch study, none of the subjects reported primary or cumulative skin reactions [1]. No specific adverse-effect literature for the peptide on its own was identified. Reviews of cosmetic peptides discuss their use in formulations for sensitive skin, where the typical selling points are potency at low concentration and the ability to interact with skin cells by multiple mechanisms [3].
Active research concerns delivery: nanoparticle carriers [2], hydrogels [5] and microneedle patches [1] are all being used to improve how cosmetic peptides reach the skin.

timeline.event: Palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (Matrixyl) launched by Sederma, an early signal peptide cosmetic.[4]
Monocentric study of a multi-peptide microneedle patch published.[1]
Collagen nanoparticle study with palmitoyl tripeptide-5 published.[2]
